title: Losing Just 80 Minutes of Sleep a Night Leads to Weight Gain, Columbia Study Finds
excerpt: A six-week randomised trial shows that even mild, chronic sleep restriction caused participants to gain weight and become significantly more sedentary — a pattern that affects nearly a third of adults worldwide.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mild sleep restriction of 80 minutes leads to an average weight gain of one pound.
  • Participants became 17 minutes more sedentary daily, increasing to nearly 30 minutes for specific groups.
  • Weight gain was linked to reduced physical activity, not increased appetite, challenging previous beliefs.
  • Chronic sleep loss raises risks of insulin resistance and heart inflammation, especially in women.

Columbia University Study, Annals of Internal Medicine
  • Adults who slept roughly 80 minutes less per night for six weeks gained an average of one pound and added 0.52 cm to their waist circumference, according to a Columbia University study published in Annals of Internal Medicine.
  • Sedentary time increased by an average of 17 minutes per day during sleep restriction, rising to nearly 30 minutes for men and postmenopausal women — even after accounting for longer waking hours.
  • The weight gain was driven by reduced physical activity rather than increased appetite, challenging previous assumptions about why sleep-deprived people gain weight.
  • Earlier analyses of the same participants found that mild sleep loss also increased insulin resistance in women and triggered heart inflammation — suggesting cascading health risks from chronic under-sleeping.

Adults who cut their nightly sleep by about 80 minutes for six weeks gained an average of one pound and became measurably more sedentary, researchers at Columbia University reported in a study published July 6 in Annals of Internal Medicine. The findings mark a shift from decades of research that focused on extreme sleep deprivation, showing for the first time that the kind of mild, chronic sleep loss experienced by roughly 30 percent of adults can drive gradual weight gain.

What the Study Found

The research team, led by Marie-Pierre St-Onge, a professor of nutritional medicine at Columbia, pooled data from two randomised crossover trials involving 95 adults aged 20 and older who normally slept at least seven hours a night. All participants were recruited from the New York City metropolitan area between 2016 and 2023 and had elevated cardiometabolic risk factors.

Each participant completed two six-week phases: one in which they delayed their bedtime by 90 minutes — resulting in an average sleep reduction of 78.4 minutes — and another in which they maintained their usual sleep schedule. Throughout both phases, wrist-worn monitors tracked sleep duration and physical activity, while researchers measured body weight, waist circumference, body composition via MRI, and fasting levels of appetite-related hormones including leptin, ghrelin, and GLP-1.

During the sleep-restriction phase, participants gained an average of one pound (0.45 kg) and added 0.52 centimetres to their waist circumference. Sedentary time climbed by an average of 17 minutes per day — and by nearly 30 minutes per day among men and postmenopausal women.

"The main takeaway is that sustaining a reduction in sleep, to a duration that is often observed in the general population, leads to weight gain and increases in waist circumference."

— Marie-Pierre St-Onge, Columbia University

Inactivity, Not Appetite, Drove the Gain

Previous studies of severe sleep deprivation — typically restricting participants to just four hours a night — have pointed to increased appetite and overeating as the primary mechanisms behind sleep-related weight gain. But this study found something different. The weight gain under mild sleep restriction appeared to be driven largely by reduced physical activity rather than hormonal changes that stimulate hunger.

"Even when we accounted for the fact that they were awake longer when sleep was shortened, participants spent more time being inactive than when they got adequate sleep," said Faris Zuraikat, assistant professor of nutritional medicine at Columbia and first author of the study. "This is notable, as people who are more sedentary have elevated risk for chronic diseases."

The distinction matters because it suggests that simply managing diet may not be enough to counteract the effects of insufficient sleep. Physical activity also declines — and the decline persists even when accounting for extra waking hours.

A Pattern With Cascading Health Risks

The weight gain is just one piece of a broader picture. In previous analyses of the same participant group, St-Onge's team found that women with elevated cardiometabolic risk who reduced their sleep by about 80 minutes a night developed increased insulin resistance — a precursor to type 2 diabetes. The effect was especially pronounced in postmenopausal women. A separate analysis found an influx of inflammatory cells in the heart among participants with elevated cardiovascular risk.

"Though more research is needed to further understand how sleep restriction leads to weight gain, all of our findings suggest that insufficient sleep increases the risk of obesity-related conditions like type 2 diabetes and heart disease," St-Onge said.

Why This Matters for Indians

The findings carry particular weight for Indian communities at home and abroad. A survey released on World Sleep Day in March 2026 by LocalCircles found that 46 percent of Indian adults sleep less than six hours a night — well below the seven-to-nine-hour range recommended by health authorities. Fitbit data has previously ranked India as the second most sleep-deprived nation globally, behind only Japan, with Indians averaging just seven hours and one minute of sleep and logging the world's lowest rapid eye movement (REM) sleep at 77 minutes.

For the Indian diaspora, the challenge is compounded by work schedules that often span multiple time zones — late-night calls to India, early-morning meetings in the US — creating a persistent pattern of mild sleep loss that mirrors the study's conditions closely.

What Comes Next

The Columbia team plans to study whether improving sleep in people who routinely get too little can reverse the associated weight gain and metabolic risks. Zuraikat noted that when the study's one-pound, six-week finding is extrapolated over a full year, "we would expect that losing less than an hour and a half of sleep per night could result in clinically meaningful weight gain."

St-Onge recommended personalised approaches to extending sleep: counting backward from a fixed wake time to find an earlier bedtime, reducing evening screen time and caffeine, and making incremental increases rather than dramatic shifts. "Spending more time in bed is essential to achieving longer sleep but this is not beneficial if the person is lying awake in bed, trying to sleep," she said.

Health Risks from Sleep Restriction
›Increased insulin resistance in women.
›Higher heart inflammation risk observed.
›Chronic sleep loss linked to obesity-related conditions.
